groups.content:
The escape to Varennes

The escape of Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette was planned mainly by a [27] of the queen, Axel von Fersen. Fersen wanted the family to travel separately, but the king and queen insisted on travelling as one [28]. The children's governess adopted a [29] as a Russian noblewoman. The coach made [30], and the soldiers who were supposed to meet it had left by the time it arrived. After the royal family were arrested, their return to Paris was a [31], as silent crowds watched them pass.

groups.instruction:
Questions 32-35

Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 3?

In boxes 32-35 on your answer sheet, write

YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer
NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer
NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this

questions.explanation: Answer: fertiliser Paragraph 1: labourers 'sold the contents to farmers outside the city as fertiliser '.
Answer: pump Paragraph 2: Snow 'traced many of the cases in Soho to a single public pump in Broad Street'.
Answer: curtains Paragraph 3: in Parliament 'the curtains were soaked in chemicals'.
Answer: borrowing Paragraph 3: 'The money, some £3 million, was raised by borrowing '.
Answer: tide Paragraph 4: waste was 'released into the river on the outgoing tide '.
Answer: Portland Paragraph 6: 'He insisted on using Portland cement, which was stronger than the cements traditionally used'.
Answer: FALSE Houses had to connect to sewers, but ' they emptied directly into the River Thames ', so more waste reached the river, not less.
Answer: NOT GIVEN The passage says £3 million was borrowed, but gives no estimate or final cost to compare.
Answer: TRUE ' Most of the system relied on gravity '; pumping was needed only 'at certain points'.
Answer: TRUE He doubled the pipe size, and ' His decision is the main reason why the system was still able to cope a century later '.
Answer: FALSE It 'was still relatively new', and ' some engineers of the time regarded [it] with suspicion '.
Answer: FALSE The 1866 outbreak occurred ' in part of the East End that had not yet been connected to the new system '.
Answer: NOT GIVEN The passage says only that it 'came into operation in 2025'; nothing is said about its schedule.
Answer: A Section A: their future is questioned, and ' some politicians argue that libraries are an expensive luxury '.
Answer: F Section F: ' the average electric drill is used for only around thirteen minutes in its entire lifetime '.
Answer: E Section E: Oodi ' offers 3D printers, sewing machines, music recording studios , kitchens... and rooms for playing video games'.
Answer: D Section D describes mid-twentieth-century libraries: limited opening hours, fixed shelving, 'difficult to adapt'.
Answer: ships Section B: 'books found on ships arriving in the city's harbour were taken and copied'.
Answer: tomb Section B: it 'served as his father's tomb as well as a library'.
Answer: scrolls Section B: 'It is thought to have held around 12,000 scrolls .'
Answer: theft Section C: books were chained 'to prevent theft '.
Answer: maintenance Section C: towns had to provide the land and 'pay for the library's maintenance '.

text.en: They were expensive to build.
They were too small for their collections.
They were not open at convenient times.
They were designed for too narrow a purpose.
They were built from poor-quality materials.

questions.explanation: Answer: C, D They ' were designed mainly as places to store and lend books ' (D), and ' many closed in the evenings and at weekends , precisely when working people had the time to visit' (C). Concrete is mentioned, but not as poor quality.

text.en: providing quieter places for study
bringing different groups in society together
attracting funding from private companies
reducing the cost of producing books
helping people to buy fewer goods

questions.explanation: Answer: B, E ' Such spaces help to bring people from very different backgrounds together ' (B), and by sharing things ' residents can reduce the amount they buy and throw away ' (E).
Answer: H (loyal friend) Fersen was ' a Swedish count who was devoted to the queen '.
Answer: J (family group) ' the king and queen refused to be parted from each other or from their children ', so they travelled together.
Answer: F (false identity) ' the governess travelled as a Russian noblewoman, the Baroness de Korff '.
Answer: B (slow progress) After many small delays, ' the coach was several hours behind schedule '.
Answer: D (public humiliation) Crowds lined the roads and ' the people watched the coach in almost complete silence ': a humiliating return in front of the public.
Answer: NOT GIVEN The reviewer mentions the sources Fenn uses, but says nothing about why he decided to write the book or about any new discovery.
Answer: NO One of the pleasures of the book ' is the way it takes us inside the coach ', with many small details about the journey.
Answer: NO Fenn argues that Louis 'never intended to leave France altogether', and the reviewer says ' I found it a convincing account '.
Answer: YES ' He is also admirably fair. ' 'Neither side is presented as the villain of the story.'

text.en: to explain why the Revolution began
to describe the situation that led to the king's escape
to compare Louis XVI with other French kings
to criticise the laws passed by the Revolutionary government

questions.explanation: Answer: B The paragraph explains the king's reduced powers, life under watch, and that ' he had come to believe that he was effectively a prisoner ', then his plan.

text.en: to show that the king did not take the escape seriously
to suggest that Fersen had planned the route badly
to illustrate how the book makes the journey vivid
to argue that the escape could never have succeeded

questions.explanation: Answer: C These details illustrate ' One of the pleasures of the book ... the way it takes us inside the coach'.

text.en: He misjudged how people would react to his escape.
He deliberately misled the people of Paris.
He was afraid of the crowds on the return journey.
He regretted accepting the Revolution's reforms.

questions.explanation: Answer: A ' What the king appears not to have understood is how the escape would be seen. ' His declaration seemed honest to him but proved to Parisians he could not be trusted.

text.en: His style is sometimes too informal.
He does not take sides in his account.
He simplifies the political arguments too much.
He is more sympathetic to the ordinary people than to the royal family.

questions.explanation: Answer: B He is 'admirably fair': ' Neither side is presented as the villain of the story. ' His style is 'never casual' (A).

text.en: It does not explain why the monarchy was abolished.
It gives too little attention to the queen.
It relies too heavily on a single source.
It does not consider what might have happened if the escape had succeeded.

questions.explanation: Answer: D Fenn never asks ' what would have happened if the royal family had reached Montmédy? '. He does describe the consequences in detail (A).
